District Judge Denies Trump Request To Withhold 20,000 California Ballots

Mind you, they don’t have hard evidence that these 20,000 people are non-citizens, hence the word “likely.” Early voting is already underway in California, with 500,000 ballots having already been processed this week. Not to mention the fact that we are less than a week away from Election Day, which would mean the administration’s request would have an incredibly disruptive effect on California’s ability to count and process ballots. Carter’s ruling didn’t dissuade First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli from defending the lawsuit’s merits on Wednesday. “Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials,” Essayli wrote on social media following the ruling. “This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution.”

They don’t have hard evidence that these people aren’t citizens, but when has that ever stopped President Donald Trump and his cronies from making claims about voter fraud? The DOJ has also filed a lawsuit against Alaska to prevent the vote from being certified if the Republican candidate doesn’t win.
These fools are doing literally everything except meaningfully addressing the cost of living crisis, and then having the shocked Pikachu face when it results in people voting for the opposition.
The Trump administration has said that it would appeal Carter’s ruling, but an appeals court already declined to rule on the case because Carter hadn’t issued his ruling yet. Even if it had issued a ruling, it seemed unlikely to favor the Trump administration, as the appeals court seemed skeptical about its arguments.

sources.news_title: Judge blocks Trump administration plan to set aside 20,000 California mail ballots over disputed noncitizen claims
sources.text:
The Briefing:
- A federal judge on Wednesday refused to let the Trump administration quarantine more than 20,000 California mail-in ballots from voters it claims are likely noncitizens, warning the move would "wreak havoc" on an election already in full swing.
- The government's data collapsed on closer inspection: a DHS list of nearly 16,000 alleged noncitizen voters in Nevada fell first to 185 — and then to zero, after state officials confirmed every one of those individuals was actually a U.S. citizen.
- Judge David O. Carter ruled the administration's intervention violated constitutional protections reserving election administration to the states, and said the government already has an appropriate legal remedy for illegal voting — individual criminal charges.
A federal judge in California handed the Trump administration a sweeping legal defeat on Wednesday, blocking its effort to force state election officials to set aside more than 20,000 mail-in ballots from voters the government alleges are likely noncitizens — a decision issued with blunt constitutional language and a direct challenge to the administration's evidentiary foundation.
A Last-Minute Push That Would 'Wreak Havoc'
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, of the Central District of California, rejected the Justice Department's request in a 26-page order, warning that compelling election workers to identify and quarantine tens of thousands of returned ballots while voting was already underway would "wreak havoc" on the contest. By the time of Tuesday's hearing, more than 3.7 million California voters had already returned their mail ballots — a figure that made the government's demand all the more disruptive, in Carter's assessment. The ruling was the latest in a national campaign that has reached at least 13 states, where the administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas demanding voter records from election officials.
The Words Carter Put on Paper
Carter, a 1998 appointee of President Bill Clinton, used his written order to place the administration's conduct in stark historical context. "Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," he wrote. He went further, warning that granting the administration's request would empower any political party to "create chaos for their own political purpose to disrupt the election process" — and that over 20,000 registered Californians stood to lose a right that "generations of Americans have fought to preserve."
What the Government Was Demanding
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit against California on October 15, naming Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan as defendants. The government had given election officials 48 hours to review a list of 20,000 names and ensure their ballots were not tabulated until citizenship could be confirmed. When state and county officials declined — citing legal prohibitions and concerns about the data's accuracy — the DOJ went to court asking a judge to compel compliance. California has a universal vote-by-mail system that sends a ballot to every active registered voter, meaning tens of thousands of ballots were already being processed when the administration made its demand.
The Evidence Problem — Carter Presses Hard
One of the most consequential weaknesses in the government's case was its inability to show that the people on its list were, in fact, noncitizens. During Tuesday's hearing, Carter challenged the administration's attorneys directly. "Where is the evidence?" he pressed, and told DOJ lawyers: "The remedy as a good prosecutor is to make sure these people are prosecuted." Carter described the administration's methodology for compiling the 20,000-name list as "vague" and wrote in his ruling that he "cannot conclude that plaintiffs' process is credible."
An independent review by Los Angeles County of a sample of 200 names from the government's list found that more than half corresponded to voter registrations that were already canceled or inactive — meaning no ballot had been mailed to those individuals at all. Of the sample who had reported a birthplace, more than 38 percent listed a U.S. state. The administration had also declined to disclose the full criteria it used to compile its list, having processed California's publicly available voter data through a third-party service whose matching methodology was not made transparent to the court.
On October 19, the administration announced federal charges against 28 green-card holders in California — all of whom appeared on the broader list of 20,000 names — for allegedly registering to vote or casting ballots illegally. The charges were filed the same day DOJ refiled its emergency motion before Carter. The judge noted that the prosecution of those 28 individuals was itself evidence that the government already possesses the legal tools to fight noncitizen voting one case at a time, without disrupting the mechanics of a statewide election.
Nevada's Warning Sign — And a Key Correction to the Record
The credibility problem with the government's voter data had already surfaced months earlier in Nevada, and what unfolded there cast a long shadow over the California proceedings. The Department of Homeland Security initially announced it had identified 15,903 possible noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls. After meetings with state election officials, that figure was dramatically revised — DHS said it had manually reviewed a portion of the list and was confident in only 185 of those identifications, calling the original 15,903 the "ceiling."
But when Nevada conducted its own investigation of those 185 individuals, the result was unambiguous: state records confirmed every one of them was a U.S. citizen — not a noncitizen. The final confirmed count of noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls fell to zero. Carter referenced this episode directly in his ruling, pointing to it as proof that the federal government's matching process against immigration databases was too unreliable to serve as the basis for disenfranchising thousands of registered voters. He wrote that had Nevada accepted the government's claims at face value, "185 citizens would have been deprived of their vote."
Constitutional Lines and State Authority
Beyond the data's failings, Carter found that the administration's intervention trampled on constitutional boundaries that have long protected each state's authority to run its own elections. Carter wrote that the DOJ's approach would "create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens." He rejected the administration's framing of the lawsuit as a voter integrity measure, concluding instead that it represented an attempt by the executive branch to override state election procedures without congressional authorization — the same type of overreach Carter had previously blocked when he dismissed a separate DOJ lawsuit seeking California's unredacted voter rolls earlier this year.
The judge also put on record his concern that ordering California to segregate ballots from people on the government's list would almost certainly result in the disenfranchisement of eligible American citizens — not noncitizens — given how deeply flawed the list had been shown to be. "Constitutional rights and our democracy are at stake," he wrote. "The public interest favors their protection."
Where the Case Heads from Here
The procedural history of this fight has been nearly as striking as the legal arguments. Before Carter could hold his October 27 hearing, the DOJ attempted to leapfrog him entirely, filing an emergency motion directly with the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals after Carter declined to meet a noon deadline the department had unilaterally set for itself. The Ninth Circuit convened a rare Sunday hearing and rejected the DOJ's bid 2-1 on Monday, ruling the administration had not given the district court adequate opportunity to act. The case returned to Carter, who issued his decision the following day.
Following Wednesday's ruling, the administration is expected to seek further relief from the Ninth Circuit or potentially the U.S. Supreme Court ahead of Election Day on November 3. Carter's decision is one in a growing series of judicial setbacks for the Trump administration as it has pushed to assert greater federal control over state election administration — a campaign that officials in California, Nevada and beyond have described not as a protection for voters, but as a sustained effort to cast doubt on the integrity of an election already underway.

sources.news_title: Court denies White House bid to toss California ballots
sources.text:
The Trump administration’s bid to force California to toss the ballots of some 20,000 voters it unsubstantially claimed were “likely noncitizens” was struck down on Wednesday by a California district court amid long-standing apprehension over federal enforcement impeding elections.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Judge David Carter wrote in a 26-page ruling. “In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.”
The Trump administration’s lawsuit came as part of “Operation Protect the Vote,” an initiative the Justice Department describes as “a coordinated effort among all four California-based United States Attorney’s Offices to combat and root out fraud in U.S. elections and protect electoral integrity.” Federal prosecutors in the state charged 28 people and arrested at least 11 from its list of 20,000 last week, alleging they all registered or voted illegally.
Carter, a Clinton appointee, said Wednesday that the federal government’s demands “are indicative of a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials.”
“This was a last-ditch attempt by the Trump administration to use faulty, junk data to deprive eligible voters of their rights and manufacture a non-existent crisis,” said Virginia Kase Solomón, CEO of Common Cause, a government watchdog. The Justice Department told Carter in a Tuesday hearing that it formed its 20,000-person list entirely by checking a commercially-bought dataset containing partial California voter rolls with a government list of people who had been assigned numbers in the federal immigration system.
Less than two hours after Carter issued his order, the Trump administration filed an appeal to the Ninth Circuit, which had previously rejected its claim.
Millions of Californians have already voted in several close races, including the House contest for the state’s 22nd congressional district, between Republican incumbent David Valadao and Sen. Bernie Sanders–endorsed Democrat Randy Villegas.

sources.news_title: Trump's claims about noncitizen voting are 'not credible,' a federal judge says in a scathing decision
sources.text:
Trump's Claims About Noncitizen Voting Are 'Not Credible,' a Federal Judge Says in a Scathing Decision
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter rejected the Justice Department's demand that California officials segregate ballots from 20,000 voters it describes as "likely noncitizens."
In a July 16 letter to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said a "preliminary review" suggested there "may be as many as 190,832 non-citizens registered to vote" in her state. Weber was skeptical—for good reason, it turned out. Three months later, the Trump administration reduced that estimate by nearly 90 percent, saying about 20,000 "likely noncitizens" had received California vote-by-mail ballots.
The Justice Department gave Weber and Dean Logan, Los Angeles County's top election official, 48 hours to determine whether any of the people on the government's list were in fact citizens. Otherwise, it said, Weber and Logan should segregate those ballots and refrain from processing them until citizenship could be verified. After Weber and Logan declined to comply with the Justice Department's demands, it asked a federal judge for a temporary restraining order (TRO) requiring them to do so—a request that he rejected in a scathing opinion on Wednesday.
"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," writes U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, a Bill Clinton appointee. "This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections. If Plaintiff's last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process. Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve."
The Justice Department delivered its list of "likely noncitizens" to Logan three weeks before Election Day. At that point, Los Angeles County already had sent ballots to 5.9 million voters and processed 331,000 of them. Logan said he was "legally prohibited" from doing what the Justice Department wanted because it had failed to explain the methodology used to compile the list, raising the possibility that citizens would be denied their voting rights.
There was ample reason for that concern. On July 17, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin averred that "as many as" 15,903 noncitizens were registered to vote in Nevada. The following month, when the DHS submitted a list of allegedly illegal voters to Nevada election officials, the number had fallen to 185—99 percent lower than Mullin's original figure. It turned out that every one of those 185 voters was a U.S. citizen.
"DHS has identified over 250,000 potential non-citizens illegally registered to vote" in California, New Jersey, Nevada, and Pennsylvania, Mullin said in July. He was echoing President Donald Trump, who for years has grossly exaggerated the extent of illegal voting by noncitizens, often in service of his own vanity.
Trump has repeatedly claimed, for example, that he would have won the popular vote in 2016 but for "the millions of people who voted illegally," and in January 2024 he warned that noncitizen voters "could very well affect the next election." In a speech the night before Mullin's announcement, Trump asserted that the DHS had "identified approximately 278,000 non-citizens who are registered to vote in federal elections."
Judging from Nevada's experience, the actual number may be closer to zero. It is hard to say, because the methods used by the DHS remain hazy.
In the California case, Carter says, the DHS "purchased a voter file that appeared to reflect 'the actual voter rolls in California, that as of August 2025, may be used for the 2026 federal election.'" It "then 'enhance[d]' the voter data through a 'reliable third-party data analytics'" and used records maintained by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to find "an internal USCIS immigration number" that "may" correspond to each registered voter. "The matches are scored," Carter notes, "because 'the resulting data may be incomplete, outdated, or mismatched.'"
The DHS "then compared the potential identity matches to Department of State and Social Security Administration data to screen out U.S. citizens," Carter adds. "In the next step, a confidence level was assigned (where a high score supported a 'strong identity link') and a manual review was conducted for each match to 'determine which registered voters'" were "likely to be aliens." Then came "a 'quality review' to identify issues such as 'duplicate entries' and 'incomplete records,'" followed by "an 'enrichment process' that utilized 'additional unique identifiers' to 'improv[e]' the matching process."
The government did not initially specify the source of the "reliable third-party data analytics." But it later revealed that "the third-party platform it relied on was
Lexis Nexis," Carter notes. "It remains unknown how Lexis Nexis performed its analysis, such as how it 'linked names to Social Security numbers not available on the California public voter file.' Plaintiff likewise did not explain what its 'enrichment process' entailed or how it occurred. Plaintiff also provided 'no error rates' or 'validation against a reliable benchmark' that would enable a determination of the accuracy of its findings. Omissions of this critical information prevent an evaluation of Plaintiff's procedure, including how Plaintiff reduced its initial claim of nearly 200,000 alleged noncitizens to 20,000 individuals."
Potential sources of error include conflating people with similar or identical names and outdated records that do not reflect recent naturalization. Because it is unclear how the DHS tried to address such problems, it is not surprising that Weber and Logan did not want to rely on the Trump administration's list, especially given its pattern of dramatically reducing the putative number of illegally registered voters.
"It is well-documented that matching voter registration records with data from other
administrative databases 'presents numerous challenges,'" Carter writes. And given the potential for error, he says, "Plaintiff's allegations are not credible." He adds that the TRO sought by the Justice Department "would likely lead to voter disenfranchisement" and "would create a significant administrative burden for Defendants, leading to chaos and upending the election."
In any event, Carter says, the Trump administration does not have legal standing to seek such an order. The government's main argument was that California officials, by refusing to segregate ballots from people on its list, were interfering with its enforcement of 18 USC 611, which makes it a misdemeanor for "any alien to vote" in a federal election.
"Defendants do not 'interfere' with the United States' ability to enforce Section 611 by
administering an ongoing election in accordance with established State and Federal law, rather than assuming new obligations pursuant to a federal criminal law they are not responsible for enforcing," Carter writes. It is well established that state officials have no obligation to enforce federal law, he notes, and that they cannot be "commandeered" to do so.
Nor does the federal government need such assistance to enforce Section 611. "The very same day the United States filed its TRO [application] in this Court, the Department of Justice brought charges against 28 individuals" in California under that law, Carter notes. It is not clear how many of those defendants, who represent 0.0001 percent of California's 23 million registered voters, actually cast ballots. But "if fraudulent voting occurs," Carter says, "the United States should uphold the law and bring additional Section 611 indictments against those non-citizens it believes actually voted illegally in the current—or a prior—election."
The Constitution gives states the primary responsibility for conducting elections, subject to explicit limits imposed by Congress. But the Justice Department's actions in this case "are indicative of a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials," Carter writes. The department "has filed at least thirty-one lawsuits in federal district courts across the country seeking complete voter rolls from the States. Out of the twenty-six decided cases, the DOJ has prevailed in precisely zero."
In addition to "its failed attempt to seek State voter rolls," Carter notes, "the United States has also requested that States act based on the Executive's own lists." But "sister district courts across the country have cast doubt" on the reliability of those lists for the same reasons that Carter cites in this case.
On October 23, the Justice Department "sent letters to every county in California requiring them to set aside the votes of alleged non-citizens," Carter notes. "The letters stated that election officials 'risk significant federal scrutiny' if they failed to comply with the Government's demands. The government reiterated its threat in open court yesterday, stating that State and County election officials who do not comply with their letter risk federal charges under 18 U.S.C. § 2, which criminalizes aiding and abetting the commission of a criminal offense. The court reiterates what it said yesterday: these threats must stop."

The Trump administration’s attempts to discount the votes of tens of thousands of voters it has dubiously deemed ineligible to participate in this year’s midterm elections hit two major roadblocks on Wednesday, as officials in Washington state and a judge’s ruling in California challenged the White House’s reasoning.
In August, the administration issued a report claiming that 24,000 people who took part in the 2020 election were noncitizens. Though many observers noted major flaws in the report, the White House has continued to push its disenfranchisement campaign, sending lists of residents’ names to several states and demanding that officials segregate their ballots.
After the administration sent Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs a list of people in his state that they said should be deemed ineligible to vote, a preliminary review of the list by Hobbs’s staff found that many of its claims were erroneous. The list included several names of U.S. citizens, for example.
The list is “not reliable,” Hobbs wrote on Wednesday in an open letter to the administration. “Without individualized proof of ineligibility, it would be both irresponsible and illegal for election officials to decline to process a registered voter’s ballot.”
A “significant number” of the names on the list are people who are simply “not currently registered to vote or are on inactive status,” he said.
Hobbs was emphatic in his refusal to comply with the White House’s demands to segregate ballots.
“State and local election officials in Washington work tirelessly to administer free and fair elections,” Hobbs wrote. “They are truly heroes of democracy. … Rather than distract these dedicated public servants from their important work at this late hour with a meritless lawsuit, I strongly encourage you to revisit the deeply flawed data you provided earlier this week, identify any actual proof, and work collaboratively with my office in the weeks or months to come.”
Also on Wednesday, a federal judge ruled against the administration in a lawsuit it had filed against California. The suit seeks to segregate 20,000 ballots belonging to supposed noncitizens in that state’s upcoming elections. Notably, in paperwork filed with the court earlier this week from Los Angeles, officials discovered that a “high percentage” of the names belong to people born in the United States.
Judge David O. Carter did not mince words in his decision.
“This case is about the right of every American citizen to vote in a free and fair election,” the federal judge wrote. “Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.”
“In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too,” Carter added.
The request by the administration to segregate ballots “violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections” that could have long-term precedential consequences, Carter said.
Constitutional rights and our democracy are at stake. The public interest favors their protection. Individuals who have met the requirements of California’s voter registration laws must not be deprived of a core right merely because of unfounded allegations stemming from a procedure rife with uncertainty and errors.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable,” Carter wrote in the conclusion of his ruling. “Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process.”
The refusal by Washington state officials to comply with the administration’s demands, as well as the legal ruling from a federal judge, could be challenged by the White House. But with only a few days left before the midterms, it’s unlikely that any action — short of one that is drastic and potentially unlawful — could occur in time for an appeal.
These two events come as recent polling indicates that most Americans are skeptical that President Donald Trump will accept the final outcome of the midterm elections, especially if Democrats win one or both Houses of Congress, as they’re projected to do. Trump himself has indicated that he will only accept the results if he deems them to be “honest.”

sources.news_title: Court denies DOJ request to set aside CA mail ballots ahead of election
sources.text:
A Count You Can Trust statement on the decision supporting the protection of eligible voters’ ballots emphasizes existing election safeguards and the need for clear voter information
A Count You Can Trust, the independent nonpartisan coalition working to strengthen confidence in Los Angeles County elections, welcomes last night’s decision by U.S. District Judge David O. Carter denying the Justice Department’s request to set aside approximately 20,000 vote-by-mail ballots. The request, issued after vote-by-mail ballots had been distributed to voters, concerned ballots from individuals the federal government identified as “likely noncitizens.” The coalition supports the decision as an important step in protecting eligible voters’ ballots while California continues its established work to safeguard the vote.
“Today’s decision means eligible Angelenos who have received their ballots should feel confident when they cast their vote. Los Angeles County verifies every mail-in ballot before it is counted, and that process has not changed,” said Antonio Villaraigosa, Co-Chair, A Count You Can Trust. “No one should have to wonder whether their ballot will count, and I encourage all eligible voters to vote any time between now and November 3, by mail, at an official ballot drop box, at a county vote center or on Election Day.”
Angelenos anticipated this moment. In countywide polling released by the coalition last week, 68 percent of likely Los Angeles County voters said they were worried about politicians interfering with the election process and 74 percent worry that false rumors and misleading information spreading online could confuse voters or convince them their ballots will not count. A federal challenge to ballots already in voters’ hands, days before Election Day, is exactly the kind of moment in which those worries can take hold.
California’s election system is secure and transparent, with rigorous security and verification measures designed to ensure that every eligible vote is counted. Those protections include robust voter registration safeguards, signature verification requirements and strict chain of custody procedures for securing and processing ballots. These legal safeguards help ensure elections are secure, transparent and verifiable, and give voters opportunities to see the process for themselves.
In Los Angeles County, every returned mail ballot is checked against the voter’s registration record before it is counted. A voter whose signature cannot be matched has until 5 p.m. on November 25 to correct it, and ballots postmarked by November 3 are counted if they arrive by November 10. Los Angeles County certifies its results by December 3, and the Secretary of State certifies the statewide result on December 11.
For information on how and where to vote, go to lavote.gov.

sources.news_title: Judge denies attempt by Trump’s DOJ to exclude 20,000 California ballots from vote count • West Virginia Watch

Judge denies attempt by Trump’s DOJ to exclude 20,000 California ballots from vote count
President Donald Trump’s administration is attempting to assert authority over state-run elections in the final days before voting ends in the midterm elections. (Photo by Simone Hogan/Getty Images)
A federal judge on Wednesday denied a U.S. Department of Justice request that would have forced California to not count the ballots of 20,000 voters the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens.
The decision sets the case on a course to possibly reach the U.S. Supreme Court within days.
In a scathing decision, Judge David Carter ruled that President Donald Trump’s administration was seeking to coerce California to abandon its constitutional elections procedures and “bend to the will of the Executive Branch” — a situation the veteran judge called unprecedented.
Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, denounced the Justice Department’s lawsuit in strong terms as a threat to the ability of more than 20,000 California residents to vote. He warned the DOJ’s request would create chaos less than a week from Election Day.
“In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too,” Carter wrote.
Suits in California, Alaska
The Trump administration is mounting an aggressive legal campaign to assert authority over state-run elections in the final days before voting ends in the midterm elections. In addition to California, the Justice Department has also preemptively sued Alaska over the certification of its U.S. Senate race.
If the California lawsuit reaches the Supreme Court, an opinion that keeps alive the Justice Department effort there could encourage the Trump administration to use the same tactic in more states. On the other hand, a forceful ruling against the department could thwart any nationwide strategy to force states to set aside ballots.
The Justice Department this month provided California election officials with a list of approximately 20,000 individuals that it said were likely noncitizens registered to vote in the state. The DOJ demanded California segregate the ballots of those on the list and not count them unless they could prove their citizenship — citing a federal misdemeanor crime against noncitizen voting.
The DOJ says the U.S. Department of Homeland Security compiled the list after obtaining a public copy of California’s voter roll and checking it against government records and information from the LexisNexis research service. Officials in California and Los Angeles County have questioned the list’s accuracy and warned against relying on it to prevent the tabulation of ballots.
The U.S. Constitution assigns states the responsibility of administering elections. Congress can override state rules and regulations, but the executive branch has no unilateral power to intervene absent authority from Congress.
‘Quiet period’ cited
Carter wrote that the Justice Department’s request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states control their own elections. He also noted that the DOJ had sent California the list of 20,000 voters during a 90-day “quiet period” ahead of federal elections when election officials are prohibiting conducting mass purges of registered voters.
The Justice Department’s actions point to a “broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials,” the judge wrote. Its request likely violates both the National Voter Registration Act and the Civil Rights Act, he wrote.
The Justice Department has a “clear remedy,” Carter wrote — it can prosecute alleged noncitizen voting.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable,” Carter wrote. “Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger.”
Appeal filed
In the wake of Carter’s decision, the Justice Department filed a notice of appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. Judge denies attempt by Trump’s DOJ to exclude 20,000 California ballots from vote count
President Donald Trump’s administration is attempting to assert authority over state-run elections in the final days before voting ends in the midterm elections. (Photo by Simone Hogan/Getty Images)
A federal judge on Wednesday denied a U.S. Department of Justice request that would have forced California to not count the ballots of 20,000 voters the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens.
The decision sets the case on a course to possibly reach the U.S. Supreme Court within days.
In a scathing decision, Judge David Carter ruled that President Donald Trump’s administration was seeking to coerce California to abandon its constitutional elections procedures and “bend to the will of the Executive Branch” — a situation the veteran judge called unprecedented.
Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, denounced the Justice Department’s lawsuit in strong terms as a threat to the ability of more than 20,000 California residents to vote. He warned the DOJ’s request would create chaos less than a week from Election Day.
“In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too,” Carter wrote.
Suits in California, Alaska
The Trump administration is mounting an aggressive legal campaign to assert authority over state-run elections in the final days before voting ends in the midterm elections. In addition to California, the Justice Department has also preemptively sued Alaska over the certification of its U.S. Senate race.
If the California lawsuit reaches the Supreme Court, an opinion that keeps alive the Justice Department effort there could encourage the Trump administration to use the same tactic in more states. On the other hand, a forceful ruling against the department could thwart any nationwide strategy to force states to set aside ballots.
The Justice Department this month provided California election officials with a list of approximately 20,000 individuals that it said were likely noncitizens registered to vote in the state. The DOJ demanded California segregate the ballots of those on the list and not count them unless they could prove their citizenship — citing a federal misdemeanor crime against noncitizen voting.
The DOJ says the U.S. Department of Homeland Security compiled the list after obtaining a public copy of California’s voter roll and checking it against government records and information from the LexisNexis research service. Officials in California and Los Angeles County have questioned the list’s accuracy and warned against relying on it to prevent the tabulation of ballots.
The U.S. Constitution assigns states the responsibility of administering elections. Congress can override state rules and regulations, but the executive branch has no unilateral power to intervene absent authority from Congress.
‘Quiet period’ cited
Carter wrote that the Justice Department’s request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states control their own elections. He also noted that the DOJ had sent California the list of 20,000 voters during a 90-day “quiet period” ahead of federal elections when election officials are prohibiting conducting mass purges of registered voters.
The Justice Department’s actions point to a “broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials,” the judge wrote. Its request likely violates both the National Voter Registration Act and the Civil Rights Act, he wrote.
The Justice Department has a “clear remedy,” Carter wrote — it can prosecute alleged noncitizen voting.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable,” Carter wrote. “Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger.”
Appeal filed
In the wake of Carter’s decision, the Justice Department filed a notice of appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. A three-judge panel already denied an emergency request from DOJ on procedural grounds, but two of the judges also expressed opposition on the merits — a strong signal the department will probably lose again.
The 9th Circuit’s decision, assuming the appeals court again rules quickly, will set the stage for a final appeal to the Supreme Court.
“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.
The judge’s order came a day after an hours-long hearing in Los Angeles where Essayli argued that California was required to take action after officials were provided with evidence of likely noncitizen voters.
“What they cannot do is nothing and proceed to count the votes,” Essayli said.
Essayli said election workers could face “criminal liability” if they tabulate the ballots of suspected noncitizens — drawing a rebuke from Carter, who urged the Justice Department to drop any “threats” against state and local officials.
Carter wrote that the Justice Department had previously sent letters to election officials in California saying that they risked significant federal scrutiny if they refused the DOJ’s demands.
“The government reiterated its threat in open court yesterday,” Carter wrote, adding that “these threats must stop.”
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan have warned that segregating ballots would be logistically impossible. Complying with the DOJ’s demands would effectively derail the election and push ballot counting past a statewide Dec. 3 deadline to certify results, they said.
“Tonight’s decision makes clear that the federal government’s actions are election interference,” Jon Miller, chief program officer of Public Rights Project, which represents Los Angeles County in the lawsuit, said in a statement.
“The Department of Justice is threatening state and local election officials and disrupting their crucial work while they are in the middle of running free and fair elections,” Miller said. “These officials are stewards of our democracy, doing their jobs, following the law, and fulfilling their obligations to voters.”
But beyond the practical consequences, Weber and Logan’s lawyers have argued that the Justice Department is seeking to encroach on the state’s authority over elections.
“Their legal claim is simply not serious,” Michael Cohen, a lawyer for Weber, said.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, a Clinton appointee, denied a temporary restraining order in a 26-page ruling issued Wednesday evening, NPR reported. More than 3.7 million Californians have already voted, according to the Associated Press.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures,” Carter wrote in his order.
He wrote that the requested relief “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway” and would “discount the votes of United States citizens.”
“Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred,” the judge concluded. “If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process.”

The department quickly filed a notice of appeal. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said on X that he would seek an emergency order from the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.
“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” Essayli wrote.
The government argues that time is short. Once signatures are verified, ballots are separated from their envelopes to protect voter privacy, which makes it impossible to pull an ineligible ballot back out.
According to the order, the department hand-delivered a letter and a password-protected thumb drive on Oct. 13 to Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan. The county had already mailed about 5.9 million ballots by then.

sources.news_title: Judge: Segregating California Ballots Would 'Wreak Havoc'
sources.text:
A federal judge on Wednesday refused the Justice Department's request to force California to set aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters the federal government says are likely noncitizens, ruling six days before the midterm elections that the demand would disrupt a vote already under way and discount the ballots of citizens on the basis of unproven allegations. U.S. District Judge David Carter denied the department's motion for a temporary restraining order and allowed election officials to keep processing the flagged ballots like any others, in the most consequential court test so far of how far the administration can go in intervening in a state's count.
The department sued California and Los Angeles County on October 15, asking the court to order that vote-by-mail ballots from people on a federally compiled list be held uncounted until their citizenship was confirmed. It said the list of more than 20,000 names had been assembled with the Department of Homeland Security from federal data-matching programs run against voter rolls, and it warned county officials that continuing to process those ballots could expose them to federal scrutiny and potential criminal liability. California, which mails ballots to every active registered voter, said the list was unverified, that the state was under no obligation to re-check citizenship in response to it, and that the suit was an attempt to interfere with an election.
Carter's order sided with the state on nearly every point. The request, he wrote, "violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections." He found the department was unlikely to succeed on the merits, likely lacked standing and a cause of action, and could not use the federal criminal prohibition on noncitizen voting as authority to override California's ballot-processing rules; the remedy it sought, he added, would probably violate several federal voting statutes. He also questioned whether the 20,000 figure was accurate, and he condemned the threats against election workers, which he had earlier ordered to "cease immediately." Segregating the ballots, he wrote, "would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens." Once a vote is set aside, he said, "lasting harm has occurred."
The ruling is the second defeat for the department in a week. After Carter did not rule in time for a hearing the department wanted, it asked the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals to take the case directly; a three-judge panel convened over the weekend and on Monday declined, two to one, with Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez holding that the appeals court could not decide the matter before the trial court had, and Judge Patrick Bumatay dissenting. During that hearing Sanchez pressed the government's lawyer on how the list had been built; the lawyer said it originated with voter data purchased from California and then matched against federal records, and acknowledged gaps in the explanation given in the filings. California and Los Angeles County have complained that the government has not disclosed who supplied the list.
The department is expected to appeal again, this time on the merits, and the timing is the point. Hundreds of thousands of California ballots have already been returned; Election Day is Tuesday; and any order to segregate ballots would have to be issued and implemented within days to have effect. The administration has for months previewed a strategy of assembling lists of possibly ineligible voters from federal data and delivering them to state and county officials with warnings of legal consequences if they did not act. Court filings in the California case suggest other states are to receive similar lists, which makes Carter's reasoning on standing and federal authority the template those states' election officials will cite if the department follows through.
The administration's position is that the federal government has both the data and the duty to keep noncitizens out of federal elections, that California's universal mail system makes such checks impossible without court intervention, and that holding a ballot pending verification is a modest step that harms no eligible voter. Its critics, including the state's attorneys, argue that the list is of unknown provenance and reliability, that federal law puts the administration of elections in state hands, and that the real effect of segregating ballots on the eve of an election is to cast doubt on a count before it is finished. Carter's order adopts the second reading in full. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations," he wrote, "then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process."
For the department the case was always as much about precedent as about 20,000 ballots in one state. It has now lost at the district court and been turned away at the appeals court on procedure, with a merits appeal still possible before Tuesday. For California the outcome leaves the count exactly where it was: proceeding, with the flagged ballots inside it, under rules the state wrote. What the government does with its other lists, and whether other judges read the law as Carter did, will be decided after the votes have been cast.

Judge denies Trump DOJ attempt to exclude 20,000 California ballots from vote count
President Donald Trump’s administration is attempting to assert authority over state-run elections in the final days before voting ends in the midterm elections. (Photo by Simone Hogan/Getty Images)
A federal judge on Wednesday denied a U.S. Department of Justice request that would have forced California to not count the ballots of 20,000 voters the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens.
The decision sets the case on a course to possibly reach the U.S. Supreme Court within days.
In a scathing decision, Judge David Carter ruled that President Donald Trump’s administration was seeking to coerce California to abandon its constitutional elections procedures and “bend to the will of the Executive Branch” — a situation the veteran judge called unprecedented.
Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, denounced the Justice Department’s lawsuit in strong terms as a threat to the ability of more than 20,000 California residents to vote. He warned the DOJ’s request would create chaos less than a week from Election Day.
“In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too,” Carter wrote.
Suits in California, Alaska
The Trump administration is mounting an aggressive legal campaign to assert authority over state-run elections in the final days before voting ends in the midterm elections. In addition to California, the Justice Department has also preemptively sued Alaska over the certification of its U.S. Senate race.
If the California lawsuit reaches the Supreme Court, an opinion that keeps alive the Justice Department effort there could encourage the Trump administration to use the same tactic in more states. On the other hand, a forceful ruling against the department could thwart any nationwide strategy to force states to set aside ballots.
The Justice Department this month provided California election officials with a list of approximately 20,000 individuals that it said were likely noncitizens registered to vote in the state. The DOJ demanded California segregate the ballots of those on the list and not count them unless they could prove their citizenship — citing a federal misdemeanor crime against noncitizen voting.
The DOJ says the U.S. Department of Homeland Security compiled the list after obtaining a public copy of California’s voter roll and checking it against government records and information from the LexisNexis research service. Officials in California and Los Angeles County have questioned the list’s accuracy and warned against relying on it to prevent the tabulation of ballots.
The U.S. Constitution assigns states the responsibility of administering elections. Congress can override state rules and regulations, but the executive branch has no unilateral power to intervene absent authority from Congress.
‘Quiet period’ cited
Carter wrote that the Justice Department’s request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states control their own elections. He also noted that the DOJ had sent California the list of 20,000 voters during a 90-day “quiet period” ahead of federal elections when election officials are prohibiting conducting mass purges of registered voters.
The Justice Department’s actions point to a “broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials,” the judge wrote. Its request likely violates both the National Voter Registration Act and the Civil Rights Act, he wrote.
The Justice Department has a “clear remedy,” Carter wrote — it can prosecute alleged noncitizen voting.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable,” Carter wrote. “Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger.”
Appeal filed
In the wake of Carter’s decision, the Justice Department filed a notice of appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. A three-judge panel already denied an emergency request from DOJ on procedural grounds, but two of the judges also expressed opposition on the merits — a strong signal the department will probably lose again.
The 9th Circuit’s decision, assuming the appeals court again rules quickly, will set the stage for a final appeal to the Supreme Court.
“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.
The judge’s order came a day after an hours-long hearing in Los Angeles where Essayli argued that California was required to take action after officials were provided with evidence of likely noncitizen voters.
“What they cannot do is nothing and proceed to count the votes,” Essayli said.
Essayli said election workers could face “criminal liability” if they tabulate the ballots of suspected noncitizens — drawing a rebuke from Carter, who urged the Justice Department to drop any “threats” against state and local officials.
Carter wrote that the Justice Department had previously sent letters to election officials in California saying that they risked significant federal scrutiny if they refused the DOJ’s demands.
“The government reiterated its threat in open court yesterday,” Carter wrote, adding that “these threats must stop.”
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan have warned that segregating ballots would be logistically impossible. Complying with the DOJ’s demands would effectively derail the election and push ballot counting past a statewide Dec. 3 deadline to certify results, they said.
“Tonight’s decision makes clear that the federal government’s actions are election interference,” Jon Miller, chief program officer of Public Rights Project, which represents Los Angeles County in the lawsuit, said in a statement.
“The Department of Justice is threatening state and local election officials and disrupting their crucial work while they are in the middle of running free and fair elections,” Miller said. “These officials are stewards of our democracy, doing their jobs, following the law, and fulfilling their obligations to voters.”
But beyond the practical consequences, Weber and Logan’s lawyers have argued that the Justice Department is seeking to encroach on the state’s authority over elections.
“Their legal claim is simply not serious,” Michael Cohen, a lawyer for Weber, said.

The judge found the government had not demonstrated a likelihood of success on the merits of its claims and said the requested relief could "wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens."

In his ruling, Carter questioned whether the federal government had standing to pursue the requested relief and whether federal law provided a cause of action allowing the court to intervene in the manner sought by the DOJ.

The judge also warned that changing election procedures while voting is already underway could create confusion for election officials and risk disenfranchising lawful voters.
A significant part of the ruling relied on what courts often call the "Purcell principle," derived from the Supreme Court's 2006 decision in Purcell v. Gonzalez. That doctrine generally discourages federal courts from making last-minute changes to election rules close to an election because such changes can create voter confusion and administrative problems.
Federal courts have repeatedly invoked the principle in disputes involving ballot procedures, voter eligibility rules and election administration. For high-confidence matches, investigators attempt to connect the voter information with an alien number in USCIS systems. They then search for evidence that the person has become a naturalized citizen or may have derived citizenship through their parents or other means.
USCIS ultimately sent Homeland Security Investigations a list of more than 20,000 people it believed were both registered to vote in California and likely noncitizens. After conducting its review, HSI "reasonably believes that around 20,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in California," the lawsuit says.

President Donald Trump’s administration is attempting to assert authority over state-run elections in the final days before voting ends in the midterm elections. (Photo by Simone Hogan/Getty Images)
A federal judge on Wednesday denied a U.S. Department of Justice request that would have forced California to not count the ballots of 20,000 voters the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens.
The decision sets the case on a course to possibly reach the U.S. Supreme Court within days.
In a scathing decision, Judge David Carter ruled that President Donald Trump’s administration was seeking to coerce California to abandon its constitutional elections procedures and “bend to the will of the Executive Branch” — a situation the veteran judge called unprecedented.
Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, denounced the Justice Department’s lawsuit in strong terms as a threat to the ability of more than 20,000 California residents to vote. He warned the DOJ’s request would create chaos less than a week from Election Day.
“In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too,” Carter wrote.
Suits in California, Alaska
The Trump administration is mounting an aggressive legal campaign to assert authority over state-run elections in the final days before voting ends in the midterm elections. In addition to California, the Justice Department has also preemptively sued Alaska over the certification of its U.S. Senate race.
If the California lawsuit reaches the Supreme Court, an opinion that keeps alive the Justice Department effort there could encourage the Trump administration to use the same tactic in more states. On the other hand, a forceful ruling against the department could thwart any nationwide strategy to force states to set aside ballots.
The Justice Department this month provided California election officials with a list of approximately 20,000 individuals that it said were likely noncitizens registered to vote in the state. The DOJ demanded California segregate the ballots of those on the list and not count them unless they could prove their citizenship — citing a federal misdemeanor crime against noncitizen voting.
The DOJ says the U.S. Department of Homeland Security compiled the list after obtaining a public copy of California’s voter roll and checking it against government records and information from the LexisNexis research service. Officials in California and Los Angeles County have questioned the list’s accuracy and warned against relying on it to prevent the tabulation of ballots.
The U.S. Constitution assigns states the responsibility of administering elections. Congress can override state rules and regulations, but the executive branch has no unilateral power to intervene absent authority from Congress.
‘Quiet period’ cited
Carter wrote that the Justice Department’s request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states control their own elections. He also noted that the DOJ had sent California the list of 20,000 voters during a 90-day “quiet period” ahead of federal elections when election officials are prohibiting conducting mass purges of registered voters.
The Justice Department’s actions point to a “broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials,” the judge wrote. Its request likely violates both the National Voter Registration Act and the Civil Rights Act, he wrote.
The Justice Department has a “clear remedy,” Carter wrote — it can prosecute alleged noncitizen voting.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable,” Carter wrote. “Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger.”
Appeal filed
In the wake of Carter’s decision, the Justice Department filed a notice of appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. A three-judge panel already denied an emergency request from DOJ on procedural grounds, but two of the judges also expressed opposition on the merits — a strong signal the department will probably lose again.
The 9th Circuit’s decision, assuming the appeals court again rules quickly, will set the stage for a final appeal to the Supreme Court.
“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.
The judge’s order came a day after an hours-long hearing in Los Angeles where Essayli argued that California was required to take action after officials were provided with evidence of likely noncitizen voters.
“What they cannot do is nothing and proceed to count the votes,” Essayli said.
Essayli said election workers could face “criminal liability” if they tabulate the ballots of suspected noncitizens — drawing a rebuke from Carter, who urged the Justice Department to drop any “threats” against state and local officials.
Carter wrote that the Justice Department had previously sent letters to election officials in California saying that they risked significant federal scrutiny if they refused the DOJ’s demands.
“The government reiterated its threat in open court yesterday,” Carter wrote, adding that “these threats must stop.”
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan have warned that segregating ballots would be logistically impossible. Complying with the DOJ’s demands would effectively derail the election and push ballot counting past a statewide Dec. 3 deadline to certify results, they said.
“Tonight’s decision makes clear that the federal government’s actions are election interference,” Jon Miller, chief program officer of Public Rights Project, which represents Los Angeles County in the lawsuit, said in a statement.
“The Department of Justice is threatening state and local election officials and disrupting their crucial work while they are in the middle of running free and fair elections,” Miller said. “These officials are stewards of our democracy, doing their jobs, following the law, and fulfilling their obligations to voters.”
But beyond the practical consequences, Weber and Logan’s lawyers have argued that the Justice Department is seeking to encroach on the state’s authority over elections.
“Their legal claim is simply not serious,” Michael Cohen, a lawyer for Weber, said.

Judge denies feds' request to block 20,000 California ballots in blistering opinion
sources.text:
Judge denies feds’ request to block 20,000 California ballots in blistering opinion
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A federal judge rejected the Trump administration’s bid to stop California from counting 20,000 ballots flagged over questioned citizenship, calling its allegations ‘not credible.’
- The ruling warns that the last-minute intervention could disenfranchise eligible voters, disrupt the midterm election and invite political meddling.
- The administration said it would appeal.
A federal judge in a blistering opinion Wednesday denied a Trump administration request to immediately block California elections officials from counting the ballots of 20,000 voters whose citizenship the administration questions. The administration swiftly said it would appeal.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter ruled that the administration’s allegations were “not credible” and that the intervention it sought would violate a host of federal laws, sow chaos in the ongoing midterm election, likely lead to the disenfranchisement of legitimate voters and foster future political meddling in elections.
“This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote. “If [the Trump administration’s] last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.”
Carter, an appointee of President Clinton, wrote that never in American history “has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” and that, in bringing its suit, the Trump administration was asking the court to “believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign.”
“But California and its people are sovereign, too,” Carter wrote.
Carter’s ruling was the second to deny the Trump administration a temporary restraining order against the state and Los Angeles County this week, after a three-judge panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals denied the government’s emergency request in a separate order Monday.
Carter ruled after a 3½-hour hearing Tuesday, where a slew of attorneys for the state, county and independent voting rights groups argued against the administration’s demands.

First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli — who is the top federal prosecutor in L.A. and argued for the Trump administration at Tuesday’s hearing — wrote on X that his office had already filed notice of appeal and “will immediately seek an emergency order” reversing Carter back in the 9th Circuit.
“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” Essayli wrote.
State elections officials, other state leaders, voting rights advocates and election experts all cheered the ruling.
“For the second day this week, our country’s legal system is standing up to the President’s authoritarian attempts to remain in power unchecked and unchallenged,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said.
“Today’s ruling is yet another important victory for the rule of law and the right to vote,” said California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta. “But this fight is not over. We will keep fighting to protect California’s elections from unlawful federal interference and get this baseless lawsuit dismissed.”
Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan, whom the Trump administration sued along with the state and Secretary of State Shirley Weber, said the ruling “reinforces what we have maintained throughout this process: election integrity and the protection of eligible voters go hand in hand.”
Anna Baldwin, the director of voting rights litigation at Campaign Legal Center who argued before Carter on behalf of the NAACP and the League of United Latin American Citizens, said Carter had “affirmed what the Constitution has already made clear: The states and Congress oversee our elections, not the White House and not the Department of Justice.”
Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA School of Law, said Carter’s ruling was as sweeping a rejection of the Trump administration’s illegitimate attempts to interfere in California’s election as could possibly be written.
“The federal government lost in every way it could possibly lose. It lost on the law, and it lost on the facts, and it lost on the equities — [or] weighing the harms to the various parties,” Hasen said.
And that is appropriate given that the case was a “total overreach of federal power,” Hasen said. “The Constitution’s clear that states have the authority to run Congressional elections unless Congress passes a statute otherwise — and Congress didn’t do so here.”
The Trump administration sued California, Weber and Logan on Oct. 15 — three months after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote a letter to Weber alleging that there may be more than 190,000 noncitizens registered to vote in California, and two days after acting Deputy Atty. Gen. Trent McCotter wrote again to Weber and Logan, giving them 48 hours to set aside the ballots for the 20,000 voters on the latest list.
Much of the debate since has centered on the origins and evidence in support of that list.
California and L.A. County officials have said the list appears to be inaccurate, with Logan’s office saying its review of a subset of about 200 voters found that a substantial portion appeared to have been born in the U.S. — a claim that has been disputed by Homeland Security officials.
Elections officials from several other California counties have also raised concerns about the accuracy of smaller lists of voters derived from the 20,000 that were sent to them by Justice Department officials last week, along with a warning that they could face criminal penalties if they tabulate those votes. Officials have said the lists they received contained the names of individuals who did not appear to live in their counties or did not appear to be registered.
State officials have pointed to similar lists being rejected as inaccurate elsewhere, including in Nevada. And during Tuesday’s hearing, multiple attorneys for voter advocacy groups — including the NAACP and Mi Familia en Acción — challenged both the origins and the reliability of the Trump administration’s data, and questioned why the Trump administration has so far refused to disclose when and from whom it obtained the purchased California voter roll data it says its analysis is based on.
State and county officials have said that complying with the Trump administration’s demands would badly disrupt the election and could disenfranchise legitimate voters who are wrongly included on its inaccurate list.
Justice Department officials have defended the list, saying it is composed of 20,000 individuals whom the administration has “high confidence” are not citizens, and that that number represents the “floor” to the issue — while the earlier, 190,000-strong list was the “ceiling” and also included people the administration had suspected but had less confidence were noncitizens.
They argued that Carter should immediately bar the state and county from tabulating ballots from the flagged voters until they can prove those voters are citizens — in part because, as soon as cast ballots are received in person or removed from their envelopes, they cannot be resegregated.
Essayli has said federal authorities have “overwhelming evidence” to support their claims. At Tuesday’s hearing, he said once federal authorities obtained the purchased voter registration records from the state, they “had to enrich or enhance or add, supplement, information to the voter file, so they took the info that was on there — names, addresses — and they used a database that’s often used by law enforcement, it’s used commercially.”
However, in sworn court filings, other administration officials have acknowledged “discrepancies” with some of the records and noted that more recent reviews of the data did show some people on the list appear to have citizenship claims. Essayli told Carter, “We’re never going to stand here and tell you that everything is 100%.”
In his ruling Wednesday, Carter also focused in part on the reliability of the list, noting that the process by which the Trump administration compiled it, and the reliability of outside databases to build it, remained unclear and could not be determined to be reliable based on the record before the court — particularly given that administration lists elsewhere have been shown to be unreliable.
But Carter also touched on several other weaknesses he saw in the Trump administration’s case — weaknesses that were also hit on by the 9th Circuit panel that rejected the administration’s request Monday.
Among them, Carter found that the request violates federal law precluding altering of election rules on the eve of an election.
Judge David O. Carter seemed skeptical of a Trump administration request to immediately block California officials from counting about 20,000 ballots from voters whose citizenship the administration questions, but said he would not rule until Wednesday.
Carter wrote that prosecutors like Essayli can prosecute individuals who illegally vote — which he called a “clear remedy” to the administration’s concerns about illegal voters casting ballots — but that the administration’s demands to force the state and county to set aside 20,000 ballots at once “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.”
“The Executive Branch cannot replace the remedy Congress carefully enacted with its own unlawful and unconstitutional solution instead,” Carter wrote.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” he wrote. “This Court declines to be a party to such process.”
Carter also denounced the Justice Department’s letters to county elections officials threatening them with criminal penalties if they don’t comply with its demands to set the ballots aside — writing that “these threats must stop.”
An appeal, if one is filed by the Trump administration, would face a “tough road ahead,” Hasen said.
While not guaranteed, the appeal is likely to be taken back up by the same three-judge appellate panel who previously heard — and rejected — the administration’s emergency request to block state officials from counting the ballots.
That panel — composed of two appointees of President Trump and one of President Biden — denied the previous request narrowly, ruling 2 to 1 that it did not have jurisdiction over the matter because Carter had not had a chance to rule in the lower court. However, both judges in the majority — Mark J. Bennett, one of the Trump appointees, and Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, the Biden appointee — wrote separately from the court decision to make clear that they would have denied the administration’s request on the merits too.
Among other things, they wrote that the U.S. Constitution gives power over elections to the states and Congress, not the executive branch, and that federal law precludes such voting probes so close to an election.
