As of Tuesday, over 4 million mail ballots had been returned to election offices statewide, including more than 767,000 in L.A. County alone, according to the California secretary of state.
During Tuesday’s hearing, Essayli stressed the urgent need for a resolution, noting the massive number of marked ballots that local election offices have already received and, in many cases, started processing.
Essayli is the top U.S. prosecutor in L.A., though a federal judge ruled in a separate case Tuesday that the former Republican Assemblymember is serving in his current role illegally. Essayli disagreed, saying the president and U.S. attorney general “have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department” and that he expected the U.S. Supreme Court to ultimately decide the issue.
“I look forward to serving in my current role until then,” he said in a statement.
As for the DOJ’s case against California over the 20,000 mail ballots, Essayli said in court Tuesday the federal government was making “a very narrow request” to temporarily set aside the ballots of “those suspected to be noncitizens.”
“We have not asked to void any ballots … (or) to cancel any ballots,” Essayli said.
“What we are doing is seeking to enforce” federal laws prohibiting voting by noncitizens, he added.
“We’re not telling California what they have to do. We’re telling (the state) what they can’t do. … What they cannot do is count these ballots once they’ve been informed of these prospective noncitizen ballots,” Essayli said.
But Michael Cohen, an attorney representing the state of California, said the Trump administration used data “known to be unreliable” in compiling their list of alleged noncitizens.
The state’s legal team also said that in July, the Trump administration alleged there might be more than 190,000 noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls, but by October, that number had dropped to 20,000, further questioning the data’s credibility.
Attorneys for the state also said segregating out the 20,000 ballots would disenfranchise voters.
“What we are talking about is stripping voting rights of thousands of people,” until their innocence is proven, said Anne Bellows, an attorney for the state.
Logan, the L.A. County registrar, said in a statement last week that the county conducted a preliminary review of records after receiving the DOJ’s mid-October letter requesting the county verify the citizenship status of voters that the Trump administration suspected of being noncitizens.
Of the 20,930 records the DOJ submitted, Logan said, 7,035 (33.6%) had L.A. County addresses. And out of 200 names that the registrar’s office used as part of a sample pool, about 43% of the individuals had canceled voter registrations and more than 70% had no voting history, Logan said.
“Our office takes voter eligibility seriously, and any credible evidence of unlawful voting or attempts at disrupting elections warrants appropriate review,” Logan said, adding, “Claims of unlawful voting must be supported by verifiable evidence, not assumptions.”
In recent days, registrar offices in Orange, Riverside and San Bernardino counties have also received similar letters from the Justice Department seeking their cooperation in verifying the citizenship status of voters.
Although Carter did not rule immediately following Tuesday’s hearing on whether to grant a temporary restraining order as the Justice Department had requested, it was widely perceived that he would deny it.
Earlier this year, Carter dismissed a DOJ request that would have forced California officials to hand over the state’s full voter registration list to the federal government.
And during this week’s hearing, he questioned the need for an emergency temporary restraining order on the latest matter, saying the federal government could still indict people who voted illegally after the election since results aren’t certified until December.
The judge also appeared to reprimand members of the Trump administration, saying threats against election workers should end immediately. In recent weeks, federal prosecutors have implied that election workers who process ballots they’ve been told may have been cast by a noncitizen could be held criminally liable.
“This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately. Good night,” Carter said before exiting the courtroom Tuesday.
Now the case heads back to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.
Earlier this week, a panel of judges from the 9th Circuit, citing the fact that Carter hadn’t yet had a chance to consider the matter, declined to rule on the case after taking the rare step of holding a weekend session to hear arguments from the attorneys. The federal government had asked for the session because it wanted a decision earlier than their scheduled hearing before Carter.
But even before the appellate judges decided not to rule on the case, one of the judges during Sunday’s proceeding cast doubt on the Justice Department’s request for a temporary restraining order.
“It seems to me you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law the California Legislature has adopted,” Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, said at that appellate hearing. “How can we do that?”
“Congress and the California Legislature have said non-citizens can’t vote,” Bennett added. “This lawsuit is about, ‘We don’t like the way you’re sorting citizens from non-citizens.’ I just don’t see (federal law) telling California how to do the sorting.”
City News Service contributed reporting.

sources.news_title: Federal judge denies Trump administration's request to segregate 20,000 ballots in California
sources.text:
LOS ANGELES (KABC) -- A federal judge in California has rejected the Justice Department's push for an emergency order to have California segregate roughly 20,000 ballots belonging to individuals the Trump administration has claimed are "likely" non-citizens.
The judge warns it would "wreak havoc" on midterm elections. The ruling comes as more than 3.7 million people have already voted in the state.
"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," Judge David Carter wrote in his Wednesday order. "In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too."
In a 26-page opinion, Carter repeatedly points to previous instances in American history of government officials seeking to deprive citizens of their right to vote - which he suggests lay the foundation for the Trump administration's last-ditch effort to interfere in California's election.
"Every generation in our history has witnessed repeated clashes between those who seek to limit access to the ballot and those who fight to ensure it. In this case, the federal government seeks to segregate and exclude over 20,000 ballots. This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections. If Plaintiff's last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process. Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve."
"The Government's Application for Temporary Restraining Order is DENIED."
Prosecutors for the Justice Department said they would immediately appeal the decision.
The decision is the latest legal setback for President Donald Trump in his efforts to expand federal control over state-run elections ahead of voting that will decide control of Congress for the rest of his term.
The Republican administration sued election officials in the Democratic state in mid-October, accusing the officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state's voter rolls. The administration had asked the judge to require the state to wait to count those ballots until the voters' immigration status could be verified.
The Justice Department made a similar request in Washington state this week for the state to sequester ballots submitted by hundreds of people it suspects are not U.S. citizens. Meanwhile, another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent running for U.S. Senate doesn't win. All three states have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in Congress.
Carter's order was a forceful rebuke of the federal government's demand, arguing that segregating ballots at this time in the election would require counties to develop new methods for sorting ballots and "risk disenfranchising an untold number of voters." In other words, Carter argued, it would have the same effect as purging voters and therefore violates the National Voting Rights Act, which prohibits changes to voter rolls within 90 days of an election.
"Constitutional rights and our democracy are at stake. The public interest favors their protection. Individuals who have met the requirements of California's voter registration laws must not be deprived of a core right merely because of unfounded allegations stemming from a procedure rife with uncertainty and errors. The public interest also favors the protection of election staff, who are working diligently to ensure that all citizens can cast their votes," the judge's order continued.
"The Executive's requested relief, however, would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens. The Executive Branch cannot replace the remedy Congress carefully enacted with its own unlawful and unconstitutional solution instead. Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process."
California mails ballots to all 23 million registered voters. Court filings show over 500,000 ballots had already been processed by this week, meaning their envelopes had been verified and the ballots removed. That would make it virtually impossible to know which ballot belonged to a particular voter, Los Angeles county officials have testified.
The federal government said it would file an appeal in the case for the second time on Wednesday evening. The USA's first appeal was denied by the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, since it preempted the district court's decision. Two of the three judges also expressed overwhelming skepticism about the merits of the lawsuit itself.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli doubled down on the lawsuit's arguments Wednesday.
"Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials," Essayli wrote on social media following the ruling. "This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution."
Essayli, who argued on behalf of the federal government on Tuesday, has previously said the federal government's request wouldn't impede the election. Instead, he argued that the Justice Department was trying to prevent the "dilution" of the vote with noncitizen voters.
"Segregating a ballot does not prevent it from being counted later," Essayli said. "It is designed to preserve the status quo and prevent the infection of our election with illegal ballots."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

sources.text:
Judge denies the Justice Department's bid to stop processing California ballots
A federal judge has denied an unprecedented, emergency request by the Department of Justice to segregate thousands of California ballots in the midterm elections.
The Justice Department wants California election officials to stop processing ballots pertaining to 20,000 individuals that federal officials say are "likely" noncitizens.
State and local officials in California have countered that the DOJ's list of "likely" noncitizens is unreliable, with a preliminary analysis by Los Angeles County showing that many on the list do not have active voter registrations. The officials also claim that setting aside ballots just days before Election Day, when voting and processing mailed ballots are already underway, would be unlawful and infeasible and would disenfranchise eligible voters.
In his 26-page ruling issued Wednesday evening, U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton appointee, denied the Justice Department's request for a temporary restraining order to stop processing the ballots in question.
"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," he wrote.
Carter also expressed concern about taking action that could disenfranchise eligible voters and create chaos.
"Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred," Carter wrote at the conclusion of his order. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process."
The judge said that the federal government can address the issue by continuing to indict people for the crime of illegally voting as noncitizens. DOJ officials say in the last two months they have charged dozens of people for registering or voting without being a U.S. citizen.
The DOJ's lawsuit in California, which was filed Oct. 15, is among a flurry of unprecedented actions the department has waged in states close to Election Day, raising alarms about federal interference in state election procedures.
Like in California, on Monday federal prosecutors asked Washington state election officials to review a list of 400 registered voters the DOJ believes are likely noncitizens. And last week, the DOJ filed an unusual lawsuit in Alaska that seeks to stop the state from certifying the results in its Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses due to votes for a longshot candidate with a similar name who is accused of being a spoiler candidate.
In California's most recent motion to the court, state Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, asked the judge to take into account the circumstances of DOJ's demand. "This litigation is a precursor to further interference here in California," Bonta wrote. "The Court must not be drawn into this chilling degradation of democratic values and constitutional principles."
The Department of Justice quickly filed a notice that it is appealing Carter's denial. The matter could ultimately wind up before the U.S. Supreme Court.
"Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution," Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, wrote on X, adding that he would be seeking an emergency order from the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.
The DOJ has argued the issue is urgent since once signatures are verified on returned mail ballot envelopes, the ballots are separated from their envelopes to retain voter confidentiality, making it impossible to retrieve an ineligible ballot.
Voting by noncitizens has been shown by audits and investigations to be extremely rare.
"Tonight's decision makes clear that the federal government's actions are election interference," said Jonathan Miller, chief program officer at Public Rights Project, which is counsel for Los Angeles County.
"The district court unequivocally found that DOJ's claims are unsubstantiated, that it has no basis to bring its lawsuit, and it has presented no evidence to justify its actions. The administration claims to be protecting election integrity while, at every turn, undermining the systems and federal support that safeguard our elections," Miller said.
Bonta, California's attorney general, said in a statement the ruling is an important victory, "But this fight is not over. We will keep fighting to protect California's elections from unlawful federal interference and get this baseless lawsuit dismissed."
The accuracy of the DOJ's list of "likely" noncitizens is still an ongoing matter of dispute.
A Los Angeles County analysis of a small sample of people on the DOJ's list found that a significant portion had said in records they were born in the U.S. But U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services senior official Nicolas Bartell contested that in recent court filings, writing that his office's review of those individuals found none were U.S.-born.
Bartell did acknowledge the review found four of those people "might have a claim to U.S. citizenship."
He also provided the court additional details about the federal government's methodology in creating the list in recent court filings.
But University of Delaware political scientist Kassra Oskooi, who has been tapped as an expert witness by voting rights groups who are intervening in the case, responded in his own declaration to the court that he believes USCIS's matching protocol "is likely to be unreliable."
Carter wrote in his order the federal government's protocol "raises significant concerns" and that he could not conclude its process is credible.

sources.news_title: Judge denies federal request to segregate California ballots
sources.text:
LOS ANGELES — A federal judge rejected on Wednesday a Trump administration request to stop California from processing the ballots of up to 20,000 people over allegations they are likely noncitizens, warning it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections.
The ruling by U.S. District Judge David O. Carter comes as more than 3.7 million people have already voted in the state. Over 500,000 votes have already been counted.
The decision is the latest legal setback for President Donald Trump in his efforts to expand federal control over state-run elections ahead of voting that will decide control of Congress for the rest of his term.
The Republican administration sued election officials in the Democratic state in mid-October, accusing the officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls.
The federal government's request, Carter wrote, “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.”
The administration had asked the judge to require the state to wait to count those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. The federal government also had asked the appeals court for a quick ruling — before a district judge’s scheduled Oct. 27 hearing in the case — but that effort was rejected by the higher court.
The Justice Department made a similar request in Washington state this week for the state to sequester ballots submitted by hundreds of people it suspects are not U.S. citizens. Meanwhile, another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent running for U.S. Senate doesn’t win. All three states have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in Congress.
Carter's order was a forceful rebuke of the federal government's demand, arguing that segregating ballots at this time in the election would require counties to develop new methods for sorting ballots and “risk disenfranchising an untold number of voters.” In other words, Carter argued, it would have the same effect as purging voters and therefore violates the National Voting Rights Act, which prohibits changes to voter rolls within 90 days of an election.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred," Carter wrote. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process.”
Carter also rejected the Justice Department's argument that California was impeding the federal government's ability to enforce the law. He argued that prosecutors already demonstrated the ability to enforce election law when they arrested 28 noncitizens who had voted or registered to vote illegally.
Federal prosecutors did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment on Wednesday evening.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, who argued on behalf of the federal government on Tuesday, has previously said that the federal government’s request wouldn’t impede the election. Instead, he argued that the Justice Department was trying to “safeguard the elections.”
“Segregating a ballot does not prevent it from being counted later,” he said. “It is designed to preserve the status quo and prevent the infection of our election with illegal ballots.”

sources.text:
LOS ANGELES (CN) — A federal judge on Wednesday rejected the Trump administration’s bid to sequester as many as 20,000 possible votes by residents the government says are likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls.
U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Bill Clinton appointee, denied the Justice Department’s request to issue a temporary restraining order that would have required state election officials not to process mail-in ballots by individuals on the government’s list until they have verified that these voters are actually U.S. citizens.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter said. “In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.”
The government’s request, the judge added, violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating states have control over their elections. If this last-minute request were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process, he said.
In addition, Carter questioned the credibility of the list of purported noncitizens on California’s voter rolls that Homeland Security compiled, noting a similar list of ineligible voters in Nevada that started with about 16,000 names was dwindled down to just 185 registered voters who all turned out to be citizens.
The judge also pointed out the Justice Department, in so far as it is concerned about the integrity of elections, can, as it has been doing in recent days, prosecute individuals who violate the federal statute that makes it a misdemeanor for noncitizens to vote.
“No administration can disenfranchise thousands of individuals or disrupt an ongoing election based on highly unreliable claims of noncitizenship,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement. “Today’s ruling is yet another important victory for the rule of law and the right to vote. But this fight is not over. We will keep fighting to protect California’s elections from unlawful federal interference and get this baseless lawsuit dismissed.”
The government filed a notice of appeal shortly after Carter had issued his decision.
“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement. “This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution. The solicitor general authorized an immediate appeal. We filed our notice of appeal and will immediately seek an emergency order from the Ninth Circuit.”
The ruling comes two days after the Ninth Circuit refused the government’s emergency request for a preliminary injunction, because Carter had ignored its request to issue a decision before even holding a hearing.
U.S. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Donald Trump appointee, wrote in that ruling that even if the Ninth Circuit panel had jurisdiction over the government’s appeal, which he didn’t think they did, it was unlikely the government would prevail on the merits of its claims.
Carter in January threw out the Trump administration’s lawsuit seeking to force California to turn over its unredacted voter rolls, including registered voters’ names, addresses, Social Security numbers and voting histories. The judge said at the time it appeared the executive branch wanted to abridge the right of many Americans to cast their ballots.
In July, the Department of Homeland Security warned California that over 190,000 registered voters “may be” noncitizens. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber responded, expressing doubts about the claim and asking for the underlying data. According to Weber, the department refused.
On Oct. 13, the Justice Department sent another letter, this time threatening to sue if Weber’s office didn’t “immediately instruct the appropriate elections official to segregate” the ballots of the 20,000 suspected noncitizens from citizens — that is, to review the citizenship status of all 20,000 voters within 48 hours.
Governor Gavin Newsom said at the time the lawsuit was “a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day."
He called the demand for an injunction “a totally unprecedented request that should scare the hell out of every American,” and a play from “the dictator’s playbook."

(The Center Square) – The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on Wednesday evening denied the Trump administration’s request for a temporary restraining order to force the state to segregate mail-in ballots that the federal government thinks could have been submitted by noncitizens.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Judge David Carter, a Clinton appointee, wrote in his ruling. “In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.”
The Santa Ana, Calif.-based judge said the federal government’s request to segregate more than 20,000 ballots “violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections. If plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process. Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve.”
The Center Square reached out Wednesday evening to the White House, but did not get an immediate response.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said the ruling was an important victory for the right to vote.
Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom said California would continue to follow state and federal law as it continued to hold free and fair elections.
Earlier on Wednesday, Bonta dismissed claims of mass voter fraud by the Trump administration.
Before Carter’s ruling, Trump administration has maintained the validity of its noncitizens list.
“Twenty-eight people on that list have now been charged with federal crimes, including lying about their citizenship to register to vote,” DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels told The Center Square in an email, referring to an Oct. 19 announcement of 11 arrests by the federal government. “California refused to look at the list. The Department will use every lawful tool to ensure that only American citizens vote in American elections.”
All 28 were charged with election-related crimes going back several years and, in some cases, several decades.
Bonta, meanwhile, told reporters Wednesday in San Francisco that it’s business as usual for the state’s general election on Nov. 3.
“Your fundamental voting rights remain protected under California law, and the rules for casting your ballots have not changed,” Bonta said. “I will say that that is despite multiple efforts from the Trump administration to change those rights, to undermine your rights, including undermining your right to vote by mail.”
Bonta’s address comes after a late effort by the Trump administration to alter California’s voting process on the grounds of alleged voter fraud.
On Oct. 13, the U.S. Department of Justice told the California Secretary of State’s office that the state’s voter roll had roughly 20,000 “highly likely” noncitizen voters. State investigations into noncitizen voters have regularly shown nearly no cases. In one case, of 1.1 million voters in Nevada’s 2016 election, three individuals cast illegal noncitizen votes.
With early in-person voting and voting by mail already underway in California, the DOJ on Oct. 23 told California county election officials to set aside ballots cast by the suspected noncitizens, to be counted after the counties had verified whether the voters were citizens. A 48-hour period was set for counties to respond to the request.
The DOJ told The Center Square that the effort to separate ballots would not create confusion or distrust among voters.
“What undermines confidence is noncitizens voting,” said Pels. “Eligible citizens are not affected. We asked counties to set aside these ballots, not cancel them, until citizenship is confirmed.”
But speaking to The Center Square, county registrars across the Bay Area expressed doubt in the DOJ’s noncitizen voter list. They said they had no plan to set aside ballots or otherwise act on the DOJ’s list, adding that segregating ballots would likely put them in violation of state and federal election laws.
“Clearly it’s an attempt to do two things – one, to cause public confidence in the democratic process to be eroded, a first step towards autocracy,” Napa County Registrar of Voters John Tuteur told The Center Square. “The second is to cause voter intimidation and try to prevent people from voting.”
Tuteur added that in his 29 years as Napa County registrar, he had found only one noncitizen voter, who was an election denier attempting to test the system.
“There are some people that won’t follow the rules, and they should be held accountable,” Bonta told reporters in reference to voter fraud. “It is rare, it is isolated, it happens in one-off instances, and those people should be held accountable. But there is no widespread voter fraud.”
Editor’s Note
This story was updated Wednesday evening after the U.S. District Court in Los Angeles ruled against the Trump administration. And this article is part of The Center Square’s preview coverage of the Nov. 3 general election in California. Ballots were recently mailed to registered voters. Early voting centers have opened in some counties and will open Saturday in the rest of the state. And polls will be open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Nov. 3. For more information, see the secretary of state’s website, sos.ca.gov. For early results on the night of the election, see thecentersquare.com/ california.
On Monday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit in San Francisco dismissed an emergency appeal by the DOJ to force counties to set aside ballots cast by the alleged 20,000 noncitizen voters.
In August, the Department of Homeland Security announced a list of 250,000 suspected noncitizen voters in Nevada, California, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. In Nevada, an alleged 16,000 noncitizen voters was later reduced to just 185. Local election officials later said all 185 listed individuals were citizens.
When asked about the noncitizen voter case in Nevada, Pels pushed back, saying the federal government had not yet verified Nevada’s assertion that the 185 individuals were citizens.
“Over this past year, we’ve watched the federal administration try to take control of how Americans vote,” said Bonta. “[To] threaten to send federal law enforcement to polling places, and spread misinformation meant to make people doubt our elections, meant to sew distrust in our elections.”

sources.text:
A federal judge on Wednesday denied a U.S. Department of Justice request that would have forced California to not count the ballots of 20,000 voters the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens.
The decision sets the case on a course to possibly reach the U.S. Supreme Court within days.
In a scathing decision, Judge David Carter ruled that President Donald Trump’s administration was seeking to coerce California to abandon its constitutional elections procedures and “bend to the will of the Executive Branch” — a situation the veteran judge called unprecedented.
Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, denounced the Justice Department’s lawsuit in strong terms as a threat to the ability of more than 20,000 California residents to vote. He warned the DOJ’s request would create chaos less than a week from Election Day.
“In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too,” Carter wrote.
Suits in California, Alaska
The Trump administration is mounting an aggressive legal campaign to assert authority over state-run elections in the final days before voting ends in the midterm elections. In addition to California, the Justice Department has also preemptively sued Alaska over the certification of its U.S. Senate race.
If the California lawsuit reaches the Supreme Court, an opinion that keeps alive the Justice Department effort there could encourage the Trump administration to use the same tactic in more states. On the other hand, a forceful ruling against the department could thwart any nationwide strategy to force states to set aside ballots.
The Justice Department this month provided California election officials with a list of approximately 20,000 individuals that it said were likely noncitizens registered to vote in the state. The DOJ demanded California segregate the ballots of those on the list and not count them unless they could prove their citizenship — citing a federal misdemeanor crime against noncitizen voting.
The DOJ says the U.S. Department of Homeland Security compiled the list after obtaining a public copy of California’s voter roll and checking it against government records and information from the LexisNexis research service. Officials in California and Los Angeles County have questioned the list’s accuracy and warned against relying on it to prevent the tabulation of ballots.
The U.S. Constitution assigns states the responsibility of administering elections. Congress can override state rules and regulations, but the executive branch has no unilateral power to intervene absent authority from Congress.
‘Quiet period’ cited
Carter wrote that the Justice Department’s request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states control their own elections. He also noted that the DOJ had sent California the list of 20,000 voters during a 90-day “quiet period” ahead of federal elections when election officials are prohibiting conducting mass purges of registered voters.
The Justice Department’s actions point to a “broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials,” the judge wrote. Its request likely violates both the National Voter Registration Act and the Civil Rights Act, he wrote.
The Justice Department has a “clear remedy,” Carter wrote — it can prosecute alleged noncitizen voting.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable,” Carter wrote. “Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger.”
Appeal filed
In the wake of Carter’s decision, the Justice Department filed a notice of appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. A three-judge panel already denied an emergency request from DOJ on procedural grounds, but two of the judges also expressed opposition on the merits — a strong signal the department will probably lose again.
The 9th Circuit’s decision, assuming the appeals court again rules quickly, will set the stage for a final appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on Carter’s ruling.
The judge’s order came a day after an hours-long hearing in Los Angeles where Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, argued that California was required to take action after officials were provided with evidence of likely noncitizen voters.
“What they cannot do is nothing and proceed to count the votes,” Essayli said.
Essayli said election workers could face “criminal liability” if they tabulate the ballots of suspected noncitizens — drawing a rebuke from Carter, who urged the Justice Department to drop any “threats” against state and local officials.
Carter wrote that the Justice Department had previously sent letters to election officials in California saying that they risked significant federal scrutiny if they refused the DOJ’s demands.
“The government reiterated its threat in open court yesterday,” Carter wrote, adding that “these threats must stop.”
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan have warned that segregating ballots would be logistically impossible. Complying with the DOJ’s demands would effectively derail the election and push ballot counting past a statewide Dec. 3 deadline to certify results, they said.
But beyond the practical consequences, Weber and Logan’s lawyers have argued that the Justice Department is seeking to encroach on the state’s authority over elections.
“Their legal claim is simply not serious,” Michael Cohen, a lawyer for Weber, said.

sources.news_title: 20,000 California Ballots: Judge Rejects Trump DOJ Bid
sources.text:
A federal judge on Wednesday rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to block 20,000 California ballots from being counted, handing the Justice Department a sharp loss less than a week before the November 3 midterm elections.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter denied the Justice Department’s request for a temporary restraining order, which is an emergency court order meant to stop something from happening right away while a case plays out. The DOJ wanted California and Los Angeles County to pull aside and hold mail ballots returned by roughly 20,000 registered voters the administration claims are “likely” noncitizens, and not count them until each person’s citizenship could be verified.
Carter did not hold back. “Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” he wrote.
The political news that affects your wallet, your rights and your vote, broken down in plain language. Free in your inbox.
He also made clear what was at stake for everyday voters. “This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote. “If Plaintiff’s last minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process. Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve.”
The fight started in early October. California mailed ballots to registered voters on October 1, as state law requires. On October 13, the Justice Department sent state and county officials a list of more than 20,000 people it said were likely noncitizens and demanded that officials verify their citizenship within 48 hours or set their ballots aside. When California refused, the DOJ sued the state, Secretary of State Shirley Weber, and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan. According to Logan’s office, 7,035 of the names on the list are in Los Angeles County.
California and Los Angeles County pushed back hard on the list itself. The county reviewed a sample of 200 names and found that 112 of those registrations were already inactive or canceled, and more than 70 percent of the people sampled had no voting history in California at all. The county also said about 1 in 4 people in its sample were listed as born in the United States. The Justice Department disputes that, saying its own immigration records review found none of the people it matched from the county’s sample were born in the U.S. The administration describes its list as the product of identity matching, immigration record reviews, and law enforcement screening.
The DOJ also tried to rush the courts. After Carter scheduled a hearing for October 27, federal lawyers demanded he rule by noon the next day, giving him about 15 hours. When he did not, the department went straight to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals before Carter had even ruled. On Monday, a three judge appeals panel turned the DOJ away in a 2 to 1 vote, saying the department had come to them too early and needed to wait for the trial judge. Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, dissented.
That sent everything back to Carter’s courtroom on Tuesday for a hearing that ran more than three hours. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in the Los Angeles area, argued the government had found credible evidence of noncitizens registered to vote by mail and claimed state and county officials allowed lawful and unlawful ballots to be mixed together. Federal officials had also warned county election workers they could face criminal exposure for continuing to process ballots from people on the list.
Carter shut that down before he even ruled. “This court believe that it would be wise that any threats to state and county election employees cease immediately,” he told the DOJ at the end of the hearing.
The judge also pointed to a simpler path. Federal law already makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote in federal elections, and Carter noted the government can go after anyone who votes illegally through prosecution. California’s ballot cure deadline is December 3. A ballot cure is the window when election officials contact voters to fix problems with their ballots, like a missing or mismatched signature, before the count is final. “We can clean that up before December 3,” Carter said.
Carter is not new to this fight. In January, he threw out a separate Justice Department lawsuit that tried to force California to hand over its unredacted voter rolls, meaning the full voter list with sensitive personal information included. In that case, he ruled the department was trying to go beyond the authority Congress gave it.
The numbers show why election officials said freezing ballots now would cause chaos. More than 3 million ballots have already been cast across California, including more than 500,000 in Los Angeles County alone, according to figures cited in the case.
California is not the only target. Attorney General Todd Blanche has threatened similar lawsuits against live ballots in a number of states, and the administration sent Washington state a demand to hold ballots from more than 400 people it accused of being noncitizens illegally registered to vote. Los Angeles County warned the court that a win for the DOJ here would mean any federal agency with a list could stop the count in any county in the country.
For now, California’s ballots keep getting counted. The Justice Department is expected to take the fight back to the Ninth Circuit, but as of Wednesday, the 20,000 voters on the administration’s list remain in the count.

Federal Court Denies DOJ Request to Set Aside Ballots Ahead of November 3 General Election
Ruling affirms election procedures and reinforces protections for eligible voters
LOS ANGELES — Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk (RR/CC) Dean C. Logan welcomes today’s federal court decision denying the U.S. Department of Justice’s (DOJ) emergency request to set aside ballots cast by Los Angeles County residents based on unverified claims of voter ineligibility.
The ruling, issued by U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, reinforces Los Angeles County’s continued administration of the November 3 General Election in accordance with long-established state and federal laws, procedures, and statutory timelines.
The court emphasized that established election procedures must be respected, stating: “This Court will not deprive Californians who have met the requirements for voter registration of their fundamental right because of Plaintiff’s unfounded allegations.”
The court also identified significant legal concerns with the DOJ’s proposed actions, finding that the requested relief would likely violate several longstanding federal protections, including:
- National Voter Registration Act (NVRA): Protects voters against systematic removal efforts immediately preceding a federal election.
- Voting Rights Act: Protects the rights of eligible voters to cast ballots and have their votes counted.
- Civil Rights Act: Requires consistent standards and procedures when determining voter eligibility.
“Our office takes voter eligibility seriously, and any credible evidence of unlawful voting warrants appropriate review. But claims of unlawful voting must be supported by verifiable evidence, not assumptions,” said Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan. “Today’s ruling reinforces what we have maintained throughout this process: election integrity and the protection of eligible voters go hand in hand. Our established procedures are grounded in state and federal law, and we will continue carrying out our responsibilities with accuracy, transparency, and accountability voters deserve.”
While additional judicial review remains possible, Los Angeles County remains confident in the legal foundation of its election procedures and believes today’s detailed ruling provides a strong basis for its continued application.
Los Angeles County maintains multiple layers of safeguards throughout the election process, including voter registration verification, ballot signature verification, secure ballot processing, and opportunities for public observation. These procedures protect election integrity while ensuring every eligible voter can participate, and every valid ballot is counted accurately.
“Our focus remains on the voters we serve,” Logan added. “With Election Day approaching, we want every eligible voter to feel confident that their rights are protected, their ballots are secure, and their votes will be counted accurately. The best way to demonstrate confidence in our elections is through participation, and we encourage every voter to make their voice heard.”
Voting Continues Across Los Angeles County
Voting is underway at Vote Centers and Official Ballot Drop Boxes throughout Los Angeles County. Beginning Saturday, October 31, all 646 Vote Centers will be open, allowing voters to cast their ballots at any location in the County, regardless of where they live.
Voters may also return their completed Vote by Mail ballots at any Vote Center or one of the County’s 429 official ballot drop boxes.
On Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, Vote Centers will be open from 7 AM to 8 PM.
For official election information, voting locations, and ballot tracking resources, visit LAVOTE.GOV.
